ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory risk-based screening of all partners, general-partner entities, and all ultimate beneficial owners against FINTRAC's Canadian consolidated electronic sanctions list, the Government of Canada sanctions database under the Special Economic Measures Act and United Nations Act, the U.S. OFAC SDN List, the UN Consolidated Security Council Sanctions List, and the EU Consolidated List; enhanced due diligence is required for any politically exposed person, family member, close associate, or entity owning or controlling at least 25% of the limited partnership; records must be retained for a minimum of 5 years after termination of the business relationship or transaction, and FINTRAC thresholds for large cash and wire transfers apply if any federal reporting trigger occurs.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Names must be provided in English or French using the Roman alphabet; non-Roman script names must be transliterated into Roman alphabetic characters; statutory terminology for a limited partnership requires the name to be set in accordance with Ontario legal syntax and to include 'Limited Partnership', 'L.P.', or the French abbreviation 'S.E.C.' as permitted; punctuation and accent marks are accepted where legally prescribed.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon rejection of a proposed name, the applicant may file a written request for reconsideration with the Director of Companies and Commercial Law through the Ontario Business Registry service channel, including the original name-search receipt, a cover letter citing the pertinent statutory section, and any supporting legal argument; an administrative appeal must be initiated within 60 days of the rejection notice; if reconsideration is still unsuccessful, apply for judicial review before the Divisional Court of Ontario under the Judicial Review Procedure Act; the filing of a substitute name reservation may be made concurrently to avoid delay.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted to the extent the 'virtual office' is a physical Ontario street address maintained by an authorized registered agent through which service of process, government notices, and statutory documents can be legally accepted; a post-office box, electronic-only address, or non-Ontario address is not sufficient for a domestic Ontario limited partnership.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low for this industry (estimated below 5% annual inspection probability for an Ontario LP registered solely for the publishing of lightweight ad-monetized mobile games); inspection risk may increase only if a complaint is filed, a change of registered office occurs repeatedly, or FINTRAC or law enforcement initiates a targeted review based on unusual turnover or sanctions exposure.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Limited Partnerships Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.16, as amended (ss. 2, 3, 8, 11); Partnerships Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.5, as amended; Ontario Regulation 30/16 under the Limited Partnerships Act; and applicable provisions of the Business Information Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. B.10
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Companies and Personal Property Security Branch, Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery, Province of Ontario
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form 2 – Declaration of Limited Partnership filed under the Limited Partnerships Act
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital for an Ontario limited partnership and no escrow account requirement; capital contributions are fixed by the limited partnership agreement, and a limited partner's liability is generally capped at the agreed contribution unless the limited partner participates in the control of the business.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED that ABC GP Inc., as general partner, approves the formation of the Ontario limited partnership under the Limited Partnerships Act; that the registered office be established at the address set out in the limited partnership agreement; that the initial capital contributions be accepted, recorded, and held in the partnership's bank account; that the authorized general partner and officers be appointed to execute the Declaration of Limited Partnership, the Ontario business registration, and all ancillary filings; that the banking signatories and Canada Revenue Agency authorized representatives be appointed; and that any pre-formation acts reasonably taken on behalf of the partnership are ratified. This resolution is effective as of the date of approval.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: NUANS System administered by the Ontario Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery / ServiceOntario
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search (NUANS) request through the ServiceOntario online portal or an authorized service provider to confirm the proposed limited partnership name does not conflict with existing corporate, trademark, or business names. Select the proposed name, review the preliminary search report, and file a name reservation if the general partner wishes to secure the name for up to 90 days. Notarization is not required unless foreign-sourced identification documents are used.
required_dossiers: Completed NUANS request form
Proposed limited partnership name and alternatives
Authorization letter from the proposed general partner
Identification of the applicant or agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or flagged for similarity, submit alternate name choices, request a name review by the Ministry, or appeal the decision in accordance with the Ministry's administrative procedures; adjust the proposed name and resubmit the NUANS search.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting and Execution of Partnership Declaration and Limited Partnership Agreement
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: General Partner and legal counsel; no government filing at this stage
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the Form 2 Declaration of Limited Partnership and the underlying limited partnership agreement. Ensure all general partners and limited partners are accurately listed, the registered office address is within Ontario, and the contribution details are recorded. Execute the agreement and declaration in accordance with the internal signing authorities; notarize only where a foreign partner or foreign-issued certified copy is involved.
required_dossiers: Complete Form 2 draft
Limited partnership agreement or draft partnership terms
Consent of each general partner and each limited partner
If the general partner is a corporation, a good standing certificate or certificate of incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registry or legal counsel identifies omissions or inconsistent data, amend the Form 2 and partnership agreement, obtain fresh signatures, and re-execute the documents before submission.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing the Form 2 Declaration of Limited Partnership with the Ontario Registrar
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Companies and Personal Property Security Branch, Ontario Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery (ServiceOntario)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the executed Form 2 Declaration of Limited Partnership through the ServiceOntario online Business Registry or at a ServiceOntario counter. Pay the applicable government filing fee. Receive the registry acknowledgement or stamped copy, which confirms the statutory filing and provides the Ontario limited partnership registration number. Retain proof of filing for the partnership records and for downstream revenue agency registration.
required_dossiers: Executed Form 2 Declaration of Limited Partnership
NUANS name search report or name reservation confirmation
Registered office address for service in Ontario
Government filing fee payment confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registry issues a notice of examination or rejects the declaration, the general partner must submit a corrected Form 2 or respond to the Registrar's requisition within the prescribed period; any late-filed amendments or penalties should be remedied by paying the applicable reinstatement fee and refiling the compliant declaration.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Federal Tax Registration and Business Number Establishment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Business Registration Online and applicable CRA tax services office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Using the Ontario limited partnership registration confirmation, apply to the CRA for a federal Business Number (BN) through Business Registration Online or by completing Form RC1. Register for the GST/HST account if taxable revenue exceeds the mandatory registration threshold or voluntary registration is desirable; register for a payroll deductions account if employees are hired. Confirm the registered office and general partner contact details as the authorized representatives.
required_dossiers: Ontario limited partnership registration confirmation
Legal name, trade name, and provincial registration number
Full names, citizenship, and addresses of all general partners
Authorized contact person and CRA access code
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the CRA rejects or queries the application, verify that the legal name exactly matches the Ontario registration, correct the entity identifiers, and resubmit. If the issue persists, contact the CRA business registry help line or visit the local CRA office with the original registration documents.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Organizational Meeting, Bank Account Opening, and Post-Registration Governance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: General Partner, corporate secretary, and financial institution compliance department
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Hold the initial organizational meeting of the general partner and authorized officers. Adopt the first board/general partner resolution, execute banking resolutions, and open the partnership's bank account with the appointed signatories. Prepare the minute book, partner register, and capital contribution ledger. If the partnership will have a physical office, confirm that the office complies with municipal zoning, building, and fire safety requirements. No industrial or gaming-specific licence is required for a hyper-casual mobile game publisher.
required_dossiers: Form 2 declaration and Ontario registration certificate
Limited partnership agreement and initial resolutions
Minutes of the first organizational meeting
Bank account opening package and KYC/AML forms
Identity documents of the general partner and authorized officers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the financial institution or any regulator queries governance documents, prepare a supplemental resolution correcting any inconsistency, obtain fresh signatures from the general partner, and update the partnership register accordingly.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable — no industrial establishment is proposed for a hyper-casual mobile game publisher; if a physical office is established, the local municipal zoning authority and the Ontario Building Code enforcement office have jurisdiction over occupancy and alteration permits.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not applicable — ISIC 5820 software publishing does not require an industry-specific operating or manufacturing permit under Ontario law; a standard municipal business licence or building permit may be required solely if a physical office or server room is installed.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Ontario Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks (MECP); for federal lands or transboundary matters, Environment and Climate Change Canada
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — purely digital software publishing and administrative operations generate no industrial point-source emissions and do not trigger an Environmental Compliance Approval under Ontario Regulation 1/17 or a federal Environmental Impact Assessment under the Impact Assessment Act.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No wastewater, VOCs, or hazardous air contaminants are generated by the hyper-casual games activity. The partnership must comply with applicable municipal sewer use by-laws for sanitary discharge, Ontario Regulation 347/90 for waste management, and environmentally sound disposal of electronic waste and batteries through registered receivers. Any office HVAC or emergency generator must meet the applicable Ontario Fire Code and local air emission limits.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety compliance under the Ontario Fire Code (O. Reg. 213/07) is required for any office occupancy; structural load review under the Ontario Building Code (O. national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC). Federal registration portal: 'My Business Account' (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-login-services.html) and 'Business Registration Online (BRO)' (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/businesses/topics/registering-your-business/register.html). Ontario Ministry of Finance handles provincial employer health tax and Ontario-specific tax accounts; the Ontario Companies and Personal Property Security Branch registers the limited partnership under the Limited Partnerships Act (Form 3) as a non-tax statutory prerequisite.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1 – Ensure the Ontario limited partnership (LP) is validly constituted: deliver Form 3 (Declaration) to the Ontario Companies and Personal Property Security Branch and pay the registration fee. Step 2 – Obtain the federal Business Number (BN): complete Form RC1 'Request for a Business Number and certain program accounts' and select program account 'RT' for GST/HST. Filing channels: Business Registration Online (BRO) for representatives with an access code; by mail/fax to the CRA (address prescribed for non-resident applicants); or by telephone (1-800-959-5525 inside Canada / 1-800-665-0354 from the United States, or the applicable non-resident line). A non-resident partnership may use its foreign head-office address and, if applicable, a Canadian agent's address. Step 3 – CRA issues the BN and RT account; the GST/HST account effective date is the earlier of (a) the date registration is requested and (b) the date the LP ceases to be a 'small supplier' (i.e., exceeds CAD 30,000 in aggregate taxable supplies, including zero-rated exports, in a single quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters). Step 4 – Open an RP (payroll) program account if the LP employs individuals working in Ontario, and register with the Ontario Ministry of Finance for employer health tax if the Ontario payroll exceeds the annual exemption. Step 5 – File annual T5013 Partnership Information Return with the CRA regardless of the partners' residence, reporting income allocations to all limited and general partners. Step 6 – Non-resident corporate or individual limited partners obtain or confirm their own Canadian tax identifiers and file Part I returns (T2/T1) on their allocated shares of Canadian-source business income; partnership business income allocated to non-resident partners is taxed on a net basis in Part I (no Part XIII withholding applies to such allocations).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible. For federal and Ontario income tax purposes, a limited partnership is fiscally transparent: income is computed at the partnership level but is taxed only at the partner level (Income Tax Act, s. 96). The LP itself is not a taxpayer for income tax. However, for GST/HST purposes, the Excise Tax Act (ETA) deems the partnership to be a separate 'person', so the LP is the registrant and must charge, collect, and remit HST on taxable Canadian supplies; the partners are jointly and severally liable for the LP's net tax. A limited partner's deductible losses are restricted to the amount that the partner has at risk in the partnership (ITA s. 96(2.1)). A non-resident limited partner carrying on business in Canada through the LP remains taxable in Canada under Part I on its allocated share, subject to any applicable income tax treaty.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Not applicable — Canada does not operate a 'check-the-box' or comparable elective classification regime; entity classification follows statutory legal form. Relevant elections available to an Ontario LP include: (i) the partnership fiscal-period election under ITA s. 249.1(4), whereby the LP (through a designated member) may elect a fiscal period that differs from the default calendar year, filed with the annual T5013; (ii) voluntary registration as a GST/HST registrant by a non-resident small-supplier partnership under ETA s. 240(1), which permits immediate ITC recovery on Canadian inputs; (iii) a documented partner allocation agreement in the limited partnership agreement that satisfies CRA's reasonable allocation requirements. Hybrid-mismatch arrangements (e.g., an Ontario LP that is fiscally transparent in Canada but opaque in a foreign partner's jurisdiction) are addressed automatically by ITA ss. 18.4 and 18.5, which disallow deductions to the extent of double-dip or deduction-without-inclusion outcomes; these provisions are mandatory, not elective, and must be considered when the LP's partners include US or other foreign entities.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) — a federal value-added tax administered by the CRA; in Ontario the federal GST (5%) and provincial Ontario Retail Sales Tax component (8%) are harmonized into a single HST of 13%.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000. A person is a 'small supplier' and is not required to register unless the total worldwide taxable supplies (including zero-rated exports) exceed CAD 30,000 in the immediately preceding four consecutive calendar quarters, or in a single calendar quarter. Once the threshold is exceeded, GST/HST registration is mandatory. Zero-rated export revenues count toward the threshold. A small supplier may voluntarily register; once registered, the registrant must generally remain registered for at least one year. For the Ontario LP monetizing hyper-casual games through AdMob/AppLovin, the CAD 30,000 threshold will almost always be crossed, making registration mandatory.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Not applicable — Canada has no mandatory real-time tax clearance, fiscal QR/stamping, or continuous transaction control regime. The CRA's national e-invoicing framework is voluntary (announced 2023 rollout based on the Peppol PINT standard). A GST/HST registrant must issue and retain invoices containing the prescribed particulars under ETA s. 169(1) and the Invoicing Requirements Regulations, including the registrant's BN/RT number, the date of supply, a description of the service, the consideration, and a statement that the supply is zero-rated where applicable. GST/HST returns (GST34-1) must be filed electronically by all registrants through GST/HST NETFILE, My Business Account, or EDI; paper filing is available only in narrow exceptions. No API-based clearance or pre-approval of transactions is imposed.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: A 0% HST rate (zero-rating) applies under ETA Schedule VI, Part V, sections 7 and 10 where the Ontario LP supplies a service or intangible personal property to a non-resident recipient who is not registered for GST/HST under Part IX of the ETA, provided the supply is not performed in Canada (in the case of services) and is not in respect of real or tangible personal property situated in Canada, and the non-resident recipient is not an individual present in Canada at the time the service is rendered. For a hyper-casual game publisher, the following supplies qualify as zero-rated exports: (i) the supply of ad-placement and ad-monetization services to non-resident ad networks (AdMob, AppLovin) under the network's publisher agreement; (ii) the license or transfer of digital game software/intangible property to non-resident end users or distributors, delivered or made available electronically. To claim zero-rating, the LP must verify and document the recipient's non-resident status (normal place of business outside Canada, foreign billing address, non-Canadian incorporation), issue an invoice stating 'Zero-rated supply — ETA Schedule VI, Part V', exclude HST, and retain contemporaneous export evidence. Input tax credits (ITCs) on Canadian inputs are fully available to the LP because the zero-rated export supplies are 'commercial activity' under ETA s. 240; the GST/HST refund arises through the normal ITC mechanism, not a special refund program.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (B13A) — Not applicable to zero-rated digital services and electronically delivered intangibles (no physical goods cross the border); required only if the LP later exports media or hardware.

Bill of Lading — Not applicable to a digital services export; the functional equivalent is the platform payout/ad-serving statement issued by AdMob or AppLovin to the LP evidencing the offshore delivery of advertising inventory and the computation of publication revenue.

Inward Remittance Certificate — CRA-expected bank record, in respect of the relevant payout to the LP, showing the aggregate foreign-currency payment credited to the LP's Canadian or offshore bank account and the conversion of ad-network proceeds (USD or other FX) into CAD.
Signed publisher service agreement or platform terms executed with AdMob/AppLovin identifying the non-resident counterparty and the service scope (ad mediation, placement, bid stream access).
GST/HST-compliant invoices issued to the non-resident ad networks, marked with the LP's BN/RT account, describing the zero-rated supply, and stating 'Zero-rated: ETA Sch. VI, Pt. V'.
Monthly ad-network payout reports and bank deposit slips reconciled to the LP's sales ledger (the electronic invoice/clearance substitute for a customs declaration).

Non-resident status evidence for each ad-network counterparty: certificate of incorporation, foreign business registry extract, or written confirmation of the network's principal place of business outside Canada.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA applies heightened scrutiny to zero-rated export claims in the digital-services sector. Where the export documentation is not contemporaneous or the ad-network counterparty's non-resident status is not substantiated, the CRA may reassess the supply as taxable in Canada by applying 13% HST on the consideration, with retroactive effect from the date of supply, plus statutory interest (daily compound) under the Income Tax Act (s. 161) and the Excise Tax Act. Each GST/HST return that omits HST on a supply later determined to be taxable may be reassessed within the normal 4-year reassessment period; misrepresentation, fraud, or wilful default extends the window to 7 years. Penalties include: ETA s. 280(1) gross-negligence penalty (greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the net tax understated); ITA s. 163(2) gross-negligence penalty for income-tax understatement (50% of the understated tax) where export income is improperly excluded or zero-rated without basis; and late-filing penalties under ETA s. 280.1 and ITA s. 162 for failure to file T5013 or GST/HST returns. The 180-day repatriation benchmark is applied by the CRA as an evidentiary screen: export receivables remaining unpaid beyond 180 days may be treated as lacking economic substance and the zero-rating may be denied, leading to the full 13% HST clawback, interest, and penalties. The LP must therefore enforce payment terms with foreign ad networks, document collection efforts, and recognize receivables in accordance with ITA s. 12(2) timing rules to avoid recharacterization of the export consideration as a taxable Canadian-source financing or service amount.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (BoC) as the central monetary authority; the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) regulates federally chartered banks; FINTRAC administers anti-money laundering and cross-border transaction reporting. Canada operates no foreign-exchange control agency and leaves FX transactions to the market within the Financial Administration Act framework.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible for both current and capital account transactions. There is no statutory exchange control, no general requirement for government approval to remit dividends, interest, royalties, or profits, and no restriction on reinvestment or withdrawal of foreign direct investment. Non-resident partners in a Canadian limited partnership are subject to Canadian withholding tax on certain passive payments (e.g., Part XIII for amounts deemed to be interest, rents, or royalties) and to ordinary income tax on business carried on within Canada; however, partnership allocations of active business profits to non-residents may be taxable as Canadian-source income, requiring careful treaty analysis. Profit remittance is operationally unrestricted, provided the partnership has sufficient after-tax cash and Canadian tax clearance where mandatory.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no export-proceeds surrender requirement in Canada. Exporters and service providers, including a hyper-casual games limited partnership receiving AdMob and AppLovin USD payouts, may retain export receipts in any currency, hold them in foreign-currency bank accounts, or convert them at market rates. Cross-border wire transfers of CAD 10,000 or more must be reported to FINTRAC, but no conversion ratio or mandatory deposit timeline exists.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account for contributed limited-partner capital and operational USD/CAD clearing
Operational Account for daily receipts from mobile advertising platforms and disbursements
Foreign-Currency Account for USD receivables via correspondent clearing; Operational Account for FX settlements
Capital Escrow Account / Operational Account for partnership capital contributions
Operational Account for CAD liquidity and trade settlement
Operational Account for domestic clearing and lower-cost CAD transactions

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium legal viability with significant regulatory constraints. Offshore digital EMI platforms (e.g., non-Canadian e-money institutions) are not permitted to provide payment services to Canadian residents without compliance with the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA) as a foreign money services business (MSB) or by partnering with a Schedule I Canadian bank. They cannot serve as the sole clearing rail for partnership revenue because Canadian-dollar settlement must occur through a recognized payment system. Feasibility rating: 'Medium' for supplementary treasury purposes, provided the EMI is registered with FINTRAC, demonstrates a Canadian agent/partnership, and does not replace a full-service Tier I bank where director liability for funds segregation is appetite-expanding.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: For a newly formed Ontario Limited Partnership, the general partner (typically a Canadian corporation) and all signatories are required to undergo KYC. Most Canadian Tier I banks mandate an initial physical face-to-face interview or notarized in-person verification for accounts with foreign beneficial owners; remote opening is increasingly available but conditional on video identity verification, documentary notarization, and prior banking history. The LP must provide a registered Ontario office address; a prescribed 'registered office identification' from the Ontario Companies and Personal Property Security Act issuance is mandatory. Physical presence of at least the general partner's authorized director or a signing officer is strongly recommended for successful Tier I onboarding.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Opaque LP ownership structure with foreign, non-Canadian limited partners failing to disclose beneficial ownership
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Full limited partnership agreement, registered Ontario LP initial filing, beneficial ownership declaration disclosing every partner with 25% or more interests, passport copies of ultimate individual partners, and corporate charters/register for corporate general partners.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Digital advertising revenue from hyper-casual mobile gaming platforms flagged as high-velocity/unusual by KYC committees
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Merchant agreements and payout statements from AdMob, AppLovin, and Unity Ads; audited or CPA-reviewed revenue trail; platform tax identification certificates; monthly payout reconciliation reports; contractual evidence of ad-network business rationale.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-risk jurisdiction exposure due to foreign partner tax residency, e.g., where any limited partner resides in a FATF high-risk or monitored jurisdiction
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Tax residency certificates from the applicable treaty jurisdiction, source-of-funds documentation (three months of bank statements and asset declarations), sanctions screening results for all partners, and secondary professional reference letters from correspondent banks.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Insufficient Canadian nexus for a limited partnership whose general partner is foreign or whose registered office is only a virtual agent address
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Physical office lease or notarized Canadian agent agreement, utility bill in the LP's name, declaration of Canadian place of business, and a Canadian-resident general partner (Ontario-native P1 director) where feasible.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Pass-through partnership classification causing confusion about tax-exempt earnings and distribution obligations
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: CRA historical partnership account status, foreign tax identification number (TIN) of the entity, Form NR3010 if applicable, and a legal opinion from Canadian tax counsel confirming that limited partnership income is allocated and taxable to partners, not the entity.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Capital contributions from foreign limited partners must be wired via SWIFT MT103 or equivalent using the partnership's cash letter of instructions from its Tier I bank. Since Canada has no mandatory purpose-code framework, the remittance information field must state 'LIMITED PARTNER CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION — LP NAME' to enable internal categorization. The incoming wire amount must match the capital schedule in the LP agreement; the bank may require are Note-Copy of the LP agreement and capitalization table. All cross-border transactions greater than CAD 10,000 will be reported to FINTRAC. For hyper-casual games, capital bases are normally small (under CAD 1 million) but the same verifiability applies. Where the contribution is derived from platform profits earned offshore, the source-of-funds evidence includes the offshore parent's bank statement and board resolution designating the remittance as partnership capital.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary clearing is via SWIFT MT103 for supplier payments, contractor disbursements, and periodic distributions to non-resident limited partners. CAD payments are settled through Lynx (Canada's high-value real-time gross settlement system) or via Automated Clearing Settlement System for low-value items. Trade settlements for overseas services or licensors use Commercial Letters of Credit (MT700) plus MIRO/MT400 acceptance advice where the gaming publisher requires documentary assurance. For USD disbursements, the partnership uses a Tier I bank's US-dollar correspondent bank (typically JP Morgan or BNY Mellon for Canadian banks) to avoid double conversion; both parties settle on CLS where relevant for FX. Ad platform payouts from AdMob and AppLovin are received as Direct Deposit over ACH/SEPA/standard wire based on bank routing and SWIFT BIC, then swept into the operational account using a standing instruction.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX forwards (CAD/USD and CAD/EUR) with a Canadian chartered bank under ISDA or bilateral confirmations
Cross-currency interest rate swaps (if the partnership has any floating-rate debt or advance receivables denominated in foreign currency)
Vanilla FX options (puts/calls on CAD/USD) for revenue-side hedging without premium waiver
FX collars and zero-cost structures for locked-in convertible revenue upsides
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for exotic currency receipts (e.g., INR or BRL) where onshore delivery is constrained, executed through the bank's offshore trading desk

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T5013 Partnership Information Return and partner information slips, if CRA filing conditions are met
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within five months after the partnership fiscal year-end; filing may be mandatory based on partnership activities, partners, assets, revenue, or CRA criteria
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Generally CAD 25 per day, subject to statutory minimum and maximum penalties; repeated non-compliance may trigger CRA compliance action. No Ontario administrative strike-off applies solely for late T5013 filing.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: GST/HST return and remittance, if registered
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: According to the assigned reporting period; annual filers generally file within the applicable CRA deadline following fiscal year-end
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty and arrears interest may apply, including a penalty generally calculated by reference to tax owing and months overdue. No Ontario administrative strike-off applies.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Ontario limited partnership annual registry renewal
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No general annual return or annual renewal filing is prescribed for an Ontario limited partnership. Partnership declaration particulars must be amended when legally required changes occur.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No annual late-filing penalty or automatic annual strike-off applies because no routine annual LP return is required. Failure to update required registration information may create compliance, service-of-process, and enforcement risks.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual partnership agreement, registered office, agent-for-service, partner, and business-activity verification
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Internal governance record; Ontario Business Registry for required amendments
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Complete at least annually and file any legally required amendment promptly after the change
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No standalone annual government penalty; inaccurate or outdated registration information may impair legal notices and expose the partnership and partners to regulatory or contractual consequences.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No general Ontario statutory independent-audit requirement applies to a private limited partnership solely because of revenue, assets, or employee numbers. An audit may be required by the partnership agreement, lenders, investors, securities laws, or contractual requirements.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises may apply for general-purpose financial statements; IFRS may be used where required or selected for the reporting entity. Tax reporting follows the Income Tax Act and CRA partnership-reporting rules.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Ontario does not generally require an Ontario limited partnership to submit an annual beneficial-ownership confirmation to the Ontario Business Registry. Maintain current beneficial-ownership, partner, control, and transfer records where required by applicable tax, anti-money-laundering, lender, or contractual rules, and update them promptly after changes in ownership or control.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Partnership declaration and Ontario registration records
Limited partner and general partner register
Capital contribution, transfer, and distribution records
Minutes or written resolutions of partner decisions, where maintained
Accounting books, ledgers, financial statements, tax filings, and supporting records

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: Approximately USD 300-1,200 per year, depending on registered-office, agent-for-service, mail-handling, and compliance-support services
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 0 where no audit is required; approximately USD 3,000-15,000 for a voluntary or contractually required limited partnership audit, depending on records, transactions, and reporting complexity

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 25% combined general rate (federal Part I 15% + Ontario general corporate 10%); the Ontario Limited Partnership itself is fiscally transparent, with income allocated to partners who bear tax at their respective marginal rates
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No unconditional statutory tax holiday in Canada; eligible allocable income of a Canadian-controlled private corporation partner may benefit from the federal Small Business Deduction (9% federal + 3.2% Ontario on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income); refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (20%) and Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (40% to 60%) for qualifying game development labour; federal SR&ED investment tax credits at 15% non-refundable / 35% refundable for CCPCs; foreign tax credits for withholding taxes suffered on foreign advertising payouts

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form T5013 (Partnership Information Return) with T5013 Summary and related schedules; must be filed electronically through CRA-certified software using Internet File Transfer or the CRA's EFILE system; paper filings permitted only below the mandatory electronic filing thresholds
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual fiscal period (maximum 12 months unless CRA-approved alternative fiscal period elected)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due date is the last day of the fifth month following the partnership fiscal year-end (e.g., June 30 for a December 31 year-end); partner-level T1 returns due April 30 (June 15 for self-employed partners) and T2 returns due 6 months after corporate partner year-end

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net income or loss from the hyper-casual game publishing business: AdMob/AppLovin advertising revenue less user-acquisition costs, platform commissions, content licences, salaries, and capital cost allowance; primary operating line for the Ontario LP
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report full Canadian-source business income before partner allocation; a non-resident corporate partner is subject to Part I tax on the share of business income only if the partnership carries on business through a permanent establishment in Canada; otherwise Part XIII rules may apply

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income or loss from real estate or equipment leasing activities distinct from active game-publishing operations; generally immaterial for a pure hyper-casual studio but must be segregated if office subleases exist
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Gross rental income from Canadian real property is Part XIII-sourced; the partnership must withhold on the non-resident partner's allocable share and file Form NR601 or equivalent

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Partnership net income or loss after all deductions, including CCA, amortization, financing charges, and charitable donations; the distributive base from which each partner's share is computed
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: CRA assesses non-resident partners on the Box 4 allocation; subsection 218.1(2) requires the LP to withhold 15% of the allocated income of a non-resident individual unless the partner has filed a waiver or a Part I return covering the income

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after applying special deductions and prior-year loss carryforwards; used to determine loss balances available for allocation in subsequent years
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident partners cannot deduct Canadian provincial loss carryforwards unless they remain taxable in Ontario; the LP should attach a reconciliation note for cross-border allocations

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross revenue, cost of sales, and expense detail; requires breakdown of advertising payouts by platform (AdMob, AppLovin), platform store deductibles, and operating overhead
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include all revenues attributable to the Ontario permanent establishment; passive cross-border platform income must be separated to prevent mismatching

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Direct costs such as app-store commissions (Apple/Google at 15-30%), SDK licensing fees, server hosting, creative production, and paid-user-acquisition spend; also discloses inventory and work-in-progress for software
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Costs paid to non-resident affiliates must be contemporaneously documented and benchmarked under section 247; the schedule must cross-reference Form T106 if aggregate non-arm's length payments exceed CAD 2,000,000

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of Box 4 amounts among partners according to the limited partnership agreement, including special allocations, carried-interest mechanics, and guaranteed payments
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For each non-resident partner, enter country of residence, tax identification number, and indicate whether a valid Certificate of Residence supports a treaty-reduced rate; attach a completed Form NR301 where applicable

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Part XIII - Non-Resident Partner Withholding Schedule
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Declaration of withheld amounts under subsection 218.1(1) and aggregate Part XIII tax remitted to CRA during the fiscal period
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File Form T5013-S summary and remit withheld amounts to the CRA; failure to withhold renders the LP jointly and severally liable for the non-resident partner's unpaid Canadian tax

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of CAD 25.00 per day for each day late (minimum CAD 100.00; maximum CAD 2,500.00) under section 162; additional 5% filing penalty plus 1% per full month (up to 12 months) on any unremitted balance for non-resident partners; CAD 100 penalty for each missing or incorrect T5013 partner slip; gross negligence penalty of 50% of understated tax under subsection 163(2); criminal prosecution for wilful failure to file

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding tax on dividends paid by a Canadian resident corporation to non-resident shareholders/partners; for the Ontario LP, distributions of Canadian-source business or property income to non-resident limited partners are generally subject to 25% Part XIII withholding, subject to a 15% withholding regime under subsection 218.1(1) for non-resident individuals earning business income through the partnership, and further subject to treaty reduction
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim a reduced treaty rate, the non-resident partner must: (1) obtain an official Certificate of Residence (TRC) from the tax authority of its country of residence certifying treaty residency; (2) complete and submit Form NR301 (Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits under a Tax Treaty) to the Ontario LP or withholding agent; (3) confirm beneficial ownership and satisfy any Limitation-on-Benefits or derivative-benefits clause in the applicable DTA; (4) retain supporting documentation for CRA review; the payer may apply the reduced rate upon receipt of complete documentation or request a CRA advance withholding-tax ruling for uncertain eligibility
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII rates: interest 25%, royalties on copyrights/software 25%; typical treaty reductions under Canada-US DTA: interest 0% for arm's-length loans (15% otherwise), royalties for the use of computer software copyright 0%, all other copyright royalties 10%; non-treaty jurisdictions remain at the full 25% statutory rate; treaties with OECD jurisdictions commonly set interest at 10% and industrial royalties at 10% or 0% respectively

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 2,000,000 in aggregate fair market value of non-arm's length transactions requiring Form T106 (Information Return for Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents); CAD 1,000,000 threshold for outstanding loans or advances requiring T106 disclosure; CAD 750,000,000 consolidated group revenue threshold for Country-by-Country Report (Form RC4643) filing by the ultimate parent of an MNE group
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no jurisdiction-specific Economic Substance Regulations comparable to the UAE; however, CRA applies economic-substance analysis through the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (section 245), treaty anti-abuse provisions (beneficial ownership, limitation-on-benefits), and the OECD BEPS framework; a no-substance Ontario LP without an active office, employees, or real decision-making functions for game-publishing operations is vulnerable to GAAR recharacterization, transfer-pricing adjustments under section 247, and mandatory disclosure regime penalties; Bill C-59 amendments (in force for transactions entered into on or after January 1, 2025) impose a 50% GAAR penalty on abusive avoidance transactions lacking genuine economic substance

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Wilfully concealing or under-reporting AdMob/AppLovin advertising revenue, fabricating user-acquisition expenses, maintaining undisclosed bank or e-wallet accounts outside Canada, filing false T5013 allocations, or directing platform payouts to a foreign entity without Canadian substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Section 239 Income Tax Act: summary conviction - fine of not less than 50% and not more than 200% of the tax sought to be evaded and/or imprisonment up to 2 years; indictable conviction - fine up to 200% of tax evaded and/or imprisonment up to 5 years; civil gross negligence penalty of 50% of understated tax under subsection 163(2); failure-to-report-income penalty of 10% of unreported amounts (20% on second occurrence); compound interest charged on all outstanding balances; CRA may reopen returns beyond the normal 3-year reassessment period (10 years for misrepresentation, unlimited for fraud)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers of a corporate general partner are jointly and severally liable under subsection 227.1 for unremitted source deductions and GST/HST; subsection 160 joint liability applies to non-arm's length transfers of property made to avoid tax; a limited partner who participates in management or control of the LP forfeits limited-liability protection under the Ontario Limited Partnerships Act; criminal prosecutions target directing minds with personal fines, confiscation orders, travel-ban bail conditions, passport surrender, and extradition exposure

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing and Non-Arm's Length Transactions
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's length ad-tech intermediaries (e.g., foreign AppLovin or Google-affiliated entities) above- or below-market rates for user acquisition or IP licensing; migrating game IP to a zero-tax foreign sister corporation without compensating the Ontario LP; failing to file Form T106 when aggregate non-arm's length transactions exceed CAD 2,000,000; preparing no contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Section 247(2) discretionary transfer-pricing adjustments; penalty under subsection 247(7) of 10% of the net adjustment (reduced by the CAD 10,000 tolerance) where documentation is not contemporaneously prepared; CbC-report failure penalties of CAD 2,000 per month; general foreign-exchange and compound-interest exposure; new 50% GAAR penalty for abusive avoidance transactions entered into after 2024
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who approved or implemented the non-arm's length arrangement may be assessed under subsection 160 for property transferred without fair-market consideration; CRA may freeze corporate bank accounts and seek court orders compelling payment; a corporate general partner's directors may be personally liable for the LP's unremitted payroll and HST amounts; criminal charges may follow where documentation is intentionally falsified

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company, Sham, and GAAR Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating an Ontario LP as a pure conduit shell that lacks office premises, full-time employees, strategic decision-making, or ongoing business activity; routing hyper-casual game revenue through a tax-haven affiliate while stripping the Ontario LP of taxable profit via inflated service fees or royalty payments; entering a round-trip arrangement with a non-resident partner solely to secure treaty benefits
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GAAR under section 245 denies the tax benefit and, for transactions entered into on or after January 1, 2025, imposes a 50% penalty on the tax benefit; the common-law sham doctrine recharacterizes facade transactions with retroactive effect; mandatory disclosure regime (sections 237.3-237.6) imposes penalties up to CAD 100,000 for failing to report reportable or notifiable transactions; partnership allocations lacking economic substance may be ignored and reallocated by CRA
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Courts may pierce the veil where the LP is a pure facade or agent of its general partner; the general partner (and its directors when the general partner is a corporation) becomes personally liable for the LP's tax debts; officers may face criminal fraud charges (Criminal Code section 380) where the arrangement defrauds the Crown; travel bans, passport revocation, and arrest warrants may issue, and Ontario courts may grant anti-dissipation injunctions freezing personal assets

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Receiving high-volume AdMob/AppLovin payouts through bank or fintech rails without identifying the ultimate beneficial owners of the LP, maintaining unregistered money-service-business activity, failing to report suspicious transactions to FINTRAC, or converting advertising revenue to cryptocurrency to conceal its source
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act administrative monetary penalties up to CAD 500,000 per violation (up to CAD 1,000,000 for certain repeat violations); criminal conviction for operating an unregistered MSB carries fines up to CAD 500,000 and imprisonment up to 5 years on indictment; CRA and FINTRAC joint enforcement may result in asset seizure as proceeds of crime
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may be subject to FINTRAC administrative penalties personally for failing to implement a compliance program; knowingly facilitating money laundering creates personal criminal liability under section 462.31 of the Criminal Code with imprisonment up to 10 years; personal assets traceable to unlawful proceeds are subject to restraint orders and forfeiture; courts may impose travel restrictions and require surrender of passports pending prosecution
